steps.text: Write the introduction for our robotics paper on grasping and lifting several objects at once with a multi-fingered dexterous hand. Cover why multi-object grasping is hard, introduce our MultiGrasp framework and dataset with the contributions, then a related-work subsection and a short formal overview of the method.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Infants between 6 to 9 months of age go from a rudimentary "grabbing" technique that uses the entire hand to a more refined "pincer grasp" that uses only a subset of fingers. This development is the basis of advanced object manipulation skills, including grasping multiple objects. In the same way, in robotics there have been big advancements in multi-fingered dexterous hands, which make intricate grasping and in-hand manipulation tasks possible and improve interaction capabilities for embodied intelligence.

However, most of the existing research in robotic grasping is about single-object scenarios. Common strategies often copy the action of enveloping the object with the hand and squeezing the fingers towards it, which basically reduces the sophisticated dexterous hands to parallel grippers. This ignores the rich potential of their complex articulated structure and their kinematic redundancy.

In this work we look into the less-explored domain of multi-object grasping, which is an intricate task that needs careful management of the dexterous kinematics and dynamics of the hand. Our objective is to control a multi-fingered dexterous hand so that it grasps and lifts multiple objects placed on a table at the same time. Different from single-object grasping, multi-object grasping needs independent force closure on each object. Here each object is a separate entity with no rigid interconnection, and this gives some unique challenges:

## Diverse Configurations

Multi-object grasping covers a broad spectrum of object configurations, which depend on varying geometries, combinations and placements. The various hand configurations make this diversity even bigger, so adaptable and flexible grasping strategies need to be developed.

## Intricate Kinematics

Multi-object grasping needs the full extent of the workspace of the hand, because each object takes up a large part of it. Simple contacts with the palm or the fingertips are not enough. The entire length and the sides of the fingers have to be engaged, so the grasping pose has to be configured carefully to get force closure on each object and also avoid collisions.

## Complex Dynamics

The traditional enveloping and squeezing approach that is usually used for single-object grasping does not work for multi-object scenarios. Moving a finger to grasp one object better can put the grasp on another object at risk. So precise control and fine-tuning of the wrenches at each contact point are necessary.

To address these challenges we introduce MultiGrasp, a computational framework for multi-object grasping. As shown in Fig. 1, MultiGrasp first generates a pre-grasp pose for the given target objects. This pose is a preliminary hand configuration that serves as a goal strategy for execution. With this strategy, the framework uses an execution policy to control the hand to pick up the objects. To demonstrate this process we built Grasp'Em, a large-scale synthetic dataset with 90k diverse multi-object grasps, using the Shadow Hand. We also design a new grasp generation model that can efficiently generate pre-grasp poses for novel object configurations. For grasp execution we propose a dual-stage policy that combines motion planning for reaching and a learned policy for lifting. In simulation our method has a success rate of 44.13\% in dual-object grasping with a Shadow Hand, and it scales to more objects. Real-world experiments also validate that it is effective in practice.

In summary, the main contributions of this work are: (i) Grasp'Em, a large-scale synthetic dataset made specifically for multi-object grasping research; (ii) the first gcrl policy for grasping and lifting multiple objects at the same time; (iii) making the execution policy more adaptable to novel object configurations and imprecise pre-grasp poses, using specialist distillation and curriculum learning; (iv) the full framework MultiGrasp, which moves current robotic systems forward to multi-object grasping.

## I-A Related Work

## Generating dexterous grasping

- conditioned on objects; hard (kinematics, physical constraints); analytical vs data-driven
- analytical: early hand-/object-specific solutions; GraspIt! for arbitrary hands/objects but reach-and-squeeze, low diversity; force closure, Q_{1} -> faster, more adaptable synthesis
- data-driven: learn pose distribution, or contact points / contact maps
- human-level aims: functional, generalizable, multi-object grasping

## Multi-object grasping

- optimal hand configurations for several objects at once; two methodologies
- first: simple objects (balls, bricks, pencils), efficiency, inter-object contacts for stability; little redundancy; limited individual manipulation
- second: kinematic redundancy, different hand regions per object, detailed control
- ours closer to second: maneuver each object independently + efficiency

## Reinforcement learning

- noisy sensory inputs -> analytical solutions struggle; RL for decision-making and control
- RL manipulation mostly single-object; inadequate for dexterous grasping; conventional RL insufficient for multi-object
- gcrl for robust lifting policies, accelerated by IsaacGym

## I-B Overview of MultiGrasp

- tabletop, \mathbf{O}=\{O_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N_{o}}; O_{j} point cloud in \mathbb{R}^{N\times 3} from S(O_{j})
- find \mathcal{A}=\{a^{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} to grasp all objects; objects close enough
- pre-grasp pose H=(p,R,q); sampled by synthetic algorithm (Sec. II-A) or generative model (Sec. II-B); trajectory to H then learned lifting policy (Sec. III)

## I-A Related Work

## Generating dexterous grasping

Generating grasping poses for dexterous hands conditioned on the target objects is a complex challenge, because of intricate kinematics and physical constraints. Research here mainly splits into analytical and data-driven approaches.

Analytical methods have a long history, and early research focused on algorithmic solutions for grasping poses specific to a hand and an object. GraspIt! extended this to arbitrary hands and objects, but mostly with a reach-and-squeeze strategy, which limits how diverse the grasping poses are. Recent works introduced generalized grasp quality metrics like force closure and Q_{1}, which make grasp synthesis faster and more adaptable.

Data-driven approaches, on the other hand, learn the distribution of feasible grasping poses, or they use proxy representations like contact points and contact maps, conditioned on the characteristics of the objects.

Current research tries to reach human-level interaction capabilities, including functional grasping, generalizable grasping, and multi-object grasping.

## Multi-object grasping

The goal of multi-object grasping is to find optimal hand configurations to hold several objects at the same time. Research here mostly follows two different methodologies. The first one focuses on grasping a collection of simple objects, like balls, bricks or pencils, and cares about efficiency of the grasping process. It often relies on contacts between the objects for grasp stability. It usually does not need a lot of kinematic redundancy, so it gives efficient grasping but individual objects can only be manipulated in a limited way. The second approach uses the kinematic redundancy of the hand and engages different regions of the hand to grasp each object. This gives more detailed control over the individual objects. Our work is closer to this second approach, where the focus is on keeping the ability to maneuver each object independently while also improving overall grasp efficiency.

## Reinforcement learning

Robotic operation in complex physical environments is often hard for analytical solutions, especially because sensory inputs are noisy. In these scenarios RL has become a popular choice for decision-making and control. RL-based manipulation has mostly focused on single-object interactions. These approaches are usually not good enough for learning the intricate grasping techniques that dexterous hands need. For the complex task of multi-object grasping with dexterous hands, where diverse object configurations add more challenges, conventional RL strategies are often not sufficient. In our work we use gcrl to develop robust lifting policies, accelerated by IsaacGym.

## I-B Overview of MultiGrasp

Formally, we look at a tabletop scenario with multiple objects, denoted as \mathbf{O}=\{O_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N_{o}}. Each object O_{j} is represented as a point cloud in \mathbb{R}^{N\times 3}, which is sampled from its surface S(O_{j}). The objective is to find a sequence of hand actions, \mathcal{A}=\{a^{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}, that lets the robotic hand grasp all objects at the same time. We mainly focus on scenarios where the objects are close enough to be grasped simultaneously.

Fig. 1 shows the framework. For the given objects \mathbf{O}, a pre-grasp pose H=(p,R,q) that covers all targets is proposed, where p is the position of the hand, R its orientation, and q the joint angles. H is sampled in two ways: a detailed synthetic algorithm (Sec. II-A) and a fast generative model (Sec. II-B). Grasp execution means following a trajectory to H and then lifting the objects with a learned policy (Sec. III).

steps.text:
Infants between 6 to 9 months of age transition from a rudimentary "grabbing" technique using their entire hand to a more refined "pincer grasp" involving only a subset of fingers [1]. This developmental progression underpins advanced object manipulation skills, including the ability to grasp multiple objects [2,3]. Similarly, in robotics, significant advancements have been made in multi-fingered dexterous hands [4,5,6,7,8,9], enabling intricate grasping and in-hand manipulation tasks [10,11,12,13,14,15,16] and enhancing the interaction capabilities of embodied intelligence.

However, the majority of existing research in robotic grasping focuses on single-object scenarios [7,8,4,5,6]. Common strategies often mirror the action of enveloping the object with the hand and squeezing the fingers towards it [17,6], effectively reducing sophisticated dexterous hands to mere parallel grippers. This overlooks the rich potential of their complex articulated structure and kinematic redundancy.

In this work, we explore the less-explored domain of multi-object grasping, an intricate task that requires careful management of the hand's dexterous kinematics and dynamics. Our objective is to control a multi-fingered dexterous hand to simultaneously grasp and lift multiple objects placed on a table. Unlike single-object grasping, multi-object grasping demands independent force closure on each object. Since each object is a separate entity with no rigid interconnection, this scenario presents unique challenges:

## Diverse Configurations

Multi-object grasping encompasses a broad spectrum of object configurations, shaped by varying geometries, combinations, and placements. This diversity is further compounded by the various hand configurations, which necessitates adaptable and flexible grasping strategies [3,9].

## Intricate Kinematics

Multi-object grasping requires using the full extent of the hand's workspace, as each object occupies a significant portion of it. Simple contacts via the palm or fingertips are insufficient; instead, the entire length and sides of the fingers must be engaged [3,9]. This requires a carefully configured grasping pose that achieves force closure on each object while avoiding collisions.

## Complex Dynamics

The traditional enveloping and squeezing approach typically used in single-object grasping is inadequate for multi-object scenarios. Repositioning a finger to better grasp one object might jeopardize the grasp on another. Precise control and fine-tuning of the wrenches at each contact point therefore become imperative.

To address these challenges, we introduce MultiGrasp, a computational framework for multi-object grasping. As depicted in Fig. 1, MultiGrasp begins by generating a pre-grasp pose for the given target objects. This pose is a preliminary hand configuration that serves as a goal strategy for execution. Using this strategy, the framework employs an execution policy to control the hand in picking up the objects. To demonstrate this process, we construct Grasp'Em, a large-scale synthetic dataset of 90k diverse multi-object grasps using the Shadow Hand. We also devise a new grasp generation model [18,19] that efficiently generates pre-grasp poses for novel object configurations. For grasp execution, we propose a dual-stage policy that integrates motion planning for reaching with a learned policy for lifting. In simulation, our method achieves a success rate of 44.13\% in dual-object grasping with a Shadow Hand and scales to more objects. Real-world experiments further validate its practical effectiveness.

To summarize, the primary contributions of this work are: (i) Grasp'Em, a large-scale synthetic dataset curated specifically for multi-object grasping research; (ii) the first gcrl policy dedicated to simultaneously grasping and lifting multiple objects; (iii) an execution policy augmented for better adaptability to novel object configurations and imprecise pre-grasp poses, through specialist distillation and curriculum learning; (iv) the comprehensive framework MultiGrasp, which advances current robotic systems toward multi-object grasping.

## I-A Related Work

## Generating dexterous grasping

Conditioned on the target objects, generating grasping poses for dexterous hands is a complex challenge due to intricate kinematics and physical constraints. Research in this domain divides mainly into analytical and data-driven approaches [20].

Analytical methods have a long history, with early research focusing on algorithmic solutions for hand- and object-specific grasping poses [21,22,23,24]. GraspIt! [17] extended this to arbitrary hands and objects, though predominantly through a reach-and-squeeze strategy that limits the diversity of grasping poses. Recent works have introduced generalized grasp quality metrics such as force closure and Q_{1}, enabling faster and more adaptable grasp synthesis [7,25,26].

Data-driven approaches, in contrast, learn the distribution of feasible grasping poses [27,28,19], or use proxy representations such as contact points [29] and contact maps [6,4,30,31], conditioned on the characteristics of the objects.

Contemporary research aims at human-level interaction capabilities, including functional grasping [32], generalizable grasping [6], and multi-object grasping [9].

## Multi-object grasping

The goal of multi-object grasping is to identify optimal hand configurations for holding multiple objects simultaneously. Research in this area mainly follows two distinct methodologies. The first emphasizes grasping a collection of simple objects, such as balls, bricks, or pencils, with a focus on grasping efficiency, and often relies on contacts between objects for grasp stability [33,34,35,36,37]. It typically does not require extensive kinematic redundancy, offering efficient grasping at the cost of limited manipulation of individual objects. The second approach exploits the hand's kinematic redundancy by engaging different hand regions to grasp each object, allowing more detailed control over individual objects [9]. Our work is more in line with this second approach: we focus on keeping the ability to maneuver each object independently while also improving overall grasp efficiency.

## Reinforcement learning

Robotic operation in complex physical environments often poses significant challenges for analytical solutions, particularly because of noisy sensory inputs. In such scenarios, RL has become a favored choice for decision-making and control [38,39,40,41]. RL-based manipulation has largely emphasized single-object interactions [15,42,4,5,43], and these approaches tend to be inadequate for learning the intricate grasping techniques that dexterous hands require. For the complex task of multi-object grasping with dexterous hands, where diverse object configurations pose additional challenges, conventional RL strategies are often insufficient. In our work, we employ gcrl [44] to develop robust lifting policies, accelerated by IsaacGym [45].

## I-B Overview of MultiGrasp

Formally, we consider a tabletop scenario populated with multiple objects, denoted as \mathbf{O}=\{O_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N_{o}}. Each object O_{j} is represented as a point cloud in \mathbb{R}^{N\times 3}, sampled from its surface S(O_{j}). The objective is to find a sequence of hand actions, \mathcal{A}=\{a^{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}, that enables the robotic hand to grasp all objects simultaneously. We mainly concentrate on scenarios where the objects are close enough to be grasped simultaneously.

Fig. 1 illustrates the framework. For the given objects \mathbf{O}, a pre-grasp pose H=(p,R,q) encapsulating all targets is proposed, where p denotes the hand's position, R its orientation, and q the joint angles. H is sampled by two methods: a detailed synthetic algorithm (Sec. II-A) and a fast generative model (Sec. II-B). Grasp execution involves following a trajectory to H and then lifting the objects with a learned policy (Sec. III).
